article.title: Why More Choice Can Make a Market Feel Worse
article.framework: More Supply → More Search → Higher Comparison Cost → Reliance on Filters & Rankings → Gatekeeper Power → Market Outcome
article.coreIdea: Expanding choice creates value only when people can evaluate the additional options. As supply grows, scarcity can shift from products to attention, making search tools, rankings, and trust systems increasingly important—and powerful.
article.body:
Imagine opening a food-delivery app with five restaurants available. You can scan the options quickly, compare prices, and choose. Now imagine the same app with five thousand restaurants. The larger market clearly contains more possible matches. Somewhere inside it may be the perfect meal at the perfect price. Yet your experience can become worse, not better, because the scarce resource is no longer supply. It is your attention.

Economics often treats greater variety as a benefit because consumers with different preferences can find products closer to what they want. Digital marketplaces have pushed this logic further by making shelf space almost unlimited. An online store can list millions of products, a streaming service can host enormous libraries, and a job platform can display thousands of vacancies. But abundance creates a second problem: finding the right option.

This is a search-cost problem. Search costs include the time, effort, and information required to locate and evaluate alternatives. When there are only a few options, consumers can inspect each one. As the set expands, exhaustive comparison becomes impossible. People need shortcuts: categories, filters, reviews, recommendations, bestseller lists, or rankings.

These tools reduce friction, but they also change the market. Once consumers depend on a ranking system, being visible near the top becomes economically valuable. A restaurant on page one may receive far more orders than an equally good restaurant buried on page twenty. The marketplace is no longer merely hosting supply and demand. It is organizing attention.

This creates what we can call an attention bottleneck. In #54, we used the Bottleneck Shift Test to show that making one part of a system abundant can move scarcity elsewhere. Marketplaces illustrate the same mechanism. Digital technology makes listing capacity abundant, so the bottleneck shifts toward discovery. As discovery becomes scarce, the systems controlling discovery gain power.

Rankings are therefore not neutral decorations. They allocate a limited resource: user attention. The exact rule matters. A platform might rank products by relevance, popularity, predicted purchase probability, customer ratings, advertising payments, or some combination. Each metric creates different incentives for sellers and different experiences for consumers.

Suppose a marketplace rewards products that receive many clicks. Sellers then have an incentive to improve thumbnails, titles, and prices in ways that attract clicks. Some of this competition is useful: clearer presentation helps customers. But if clicks become the dominant proxy for quality, sellers may learn to optimize curiosity rather than satisfaction. This is another version of #49's Incentive Audit: the measured target can gradually reshape behavior around itself.

Feedback loops can amplify the effect. A product ranked highly receives more views. More views create more purchases and reviews. Those signals may cause the algorithm to rank the product even higher. Early visibility can therefore produce later visibility. Meanwhile, a new product may struggle to collect evidence of quality because few people see it in the first place.

This is sometimes called a rich-get-richer dynamic. It does not mean the popular product is bad. Popularity can contain useful information: if thousands of customers repeatedly choose and rate an item highly, that is evidence. The problem is causal ambiguity. Did the product become popular because it was better, or does it now appear better because early popularity gave it more opportunities to be chosen?

That distinction connects to our earlier causality tools. Observing that highly ranked products sell more does not prove that the ranking merely identified superior products. The ranking itself may cause some of the sales. In other words, selection and treatment are mixed together: the algorithm selects products based on expected performance, then changes performance by exposing them to more people.

Reviews provide another solution to abundance, but they introduce measurement problems of their own. A five-star average compresses many dimensions—quality, delivery, price, expectations, customer type—into one number. Two products with identical averages may have very different distributions of experiences. One may satisfy almost everyone; another may delight half its users and disappoint the rest.

The number of reviews also matters. A 4.9 rating from twelve people and a 4.7 rating from twelve thousand people carry different levels of uncertainty. Consumers often understand this intuitively, but interfaces can make the distinction more or less salient. Good marketplace design does not merely provide more information; it helps users interpret the reliability of that information.

Trust becomes especially important when quality is difficult to observe before purchase. Marketplaces may respond with verified-purchase labels, refund policies, seller histories, quality checks, or guarantees. These mechanisms are costly, but they reduce uncertainty and can support transactions that otherwise would not happen. Trust infrastructure is therefore not an optional extra. In markets with many unfamiliar sellers, it can be part of the product.

There is a business trade-off here. A platform wants enough sellers to increase variety and competition, but unlimited low-quality supply can increase search costs and weaken trust. Removing too many sellers reduces choice; admitting everyone without effective organization can create noise. The optimal marketplace is not necessarily the one with the largest raw inventory. It is the one that turns inventory into useful matches.

This extends #41's lesson on choice overload from individual psychology to market structure. As choice expands, an entire layer of intermediaries becomes more valuable. Search engines, recommendation algorithms, comparison sites, influencers, curators, and rating systems all exist partly because abundance creates demand for selection.

That layer can become a new gatekeeper. If most customers discover products through a few ranking systems, sellers must adapt to those systems. A small change in an algorithm can shift demand across thousands of businesses. Power therefore moves from controlling production or shelf space toward controlling discovery.

There are second-order effects on product design. When sellers know how discovery works, they may design not only for customers but also for the ranking mechanism. Writers think about search keywords, restaurants think about app photography, creators think about recommendation algorithms, and merchants think about review scores. The interface between seller and algorithm becomes part of competition.

Today's transferable tool is the Discovery Gap Test. Whenever supply expands rapidly, ask four questions. First, how much has the number of options increased? Second, has the user's ability to evaluate them increased at the same rate? Third, what intermediary now helps allocate attention? Fourth, what incentives and feedback loops does that intermediary create?

The framework applies far beyond shopping. Universities face thousands of applicants, employers receive enormous numbers of résumés, investors scan huge numbers of assets, and social-media users encounter more content than they could consume in a lifetime. In each case, more supply increases potential value but also raises the value of filtering.

This gives us a stock-and-flow interpretation. New options arrive as a flow. Human attention is a limited stock. Filters and rankings determine which part of that flow reaches the stock of attention. If supply grows faster than evaluation capacity, discovery becomes the scarce layer.

So “more choice” is not a complete description of a better market. Variety creates opportunity, but opportunity must be discoverable. When abundance grows, the most important economic question may shift from “Who can produce?” to “Who gets seen?” And once visibility becomes scarce, the rules that allocate it become part of the market itself.
article.summaryZh:
今天把 #41 的 choice overload 和 #54 的 Bottleneck Shift Test 推到市场层面：当商品、内容、职位或卖家数量暴增时，scarcity 会从 supply 转移到 discovery 与 attention。

核心机制是：More Supply → More Search → Higher Comparison Cost → Reliance on Filters & Rankings → Gatekeeper Power → Market Outcome。数字平台几乎消除了 shelf-space scarcity，但人的 attention 没有同步增长，于是 search cost 上升。消费者开始依赖 filters、reviews、rankings、recommendations，而这些原本只是辅助工具的系统，逐渐变成真正分配稀缺注意力的基础设施。

这直接连接 #54：abundance in one stage creates a new bottleneck elsewhere。产品供给 abundant 之后，discovery 成为 bottleneck。也连接 #49 Incentive Audit：如果 ranking 奖励 clicks，卖家就会优化 clicks；如果奖励 review score，就会围绕评分机制竞争。Metric 不只是测量市场，还会反过来塑造市场行为。

文章进一步加入 feedback loop 与 causality。高排名 → 更多曝光 → 更多购买/评价 → 更高排名，因此 popularity 既可能是 quality 的 signal，也可能部分是 visibility 的结果。看到“排名高的卖得更多”不能直接推出“算法只是准确识别了更好的商品”，因为 ranking 本身就是 treatment。

Reviews 同样涉及 measurement：4.9/5 把很多维度压成一个数字，而且 sample size 决定 uncertainty。好的平台不是单纯塞给用户更多信息，而是帮助用户判断信息可靠性。

商业上因此出现新的 trade-off：更多 sellers 能提高 variety 和 competition，但低质量供给无限增加也会提高 search cost、降低 trust。真正优秀的 marketplace 不是 raw inventory 最大，而是把 inventory 转化成 useful matches 的能力最强。

今天的新工具是 Discovery Gap Test：Supply 增长多少？→ Evaluation capacity 是否同步增长？→ 谁开始负责 filtering？→ 这个 intermediary 创造了什么 incentives 与 feedback loops？它可以迁移到招聘、大学申请、投资、社交媒体等“供给爆炸”的场景。最终问题会从“谁能生产？”转成“谁能被看见？”

speaking.question: Do you think having more choices always benefits consumers?
speaking.framework: Variety benefit → Search costs → Filtering → Quality of choice
speaking.response: Not necessarily. More choice can be valuable because people have a better chance of finding something that matches their preferences, but that only works if they can evaluate the options. When there are thousands of alternatives, search costs rise and people become more dependent on rankings, reviews and recommendations. So I think the quality of the filtering system matters almost as much as the amount of choice itself. In some cases, a smaller but well-organized set of options may actually produce better decisions than a huge catalogue.
expressions: More choice is useful only if people can evaluate the options.
The quality of filtering matters almost as much as the amount of choice.
A larger catalogue does not automatically produce better decisions.

speaking.question: Why do recommendation algorithms have so much influence on online businesses?
speaking.framework: Limited attention → Ranking → Visibility → Demand → Feedback
speaking.response: I think their influence comes from the scarcity of attention. Online platforms may contain millions of products or pieces of content, so users cannot inspect everything themselves. Recommendation systems decide what becomes visible, and visibility can directly affect demand. There is also a feedback effect: items that receive more exposure may collect more clicks, sales and reviews, which can then improve their future ranking. That means algorithms do not simply describe what is popular; they can partly shape popularity as well.
expressions: Their influence comes from the scarcity of attention.
Algorithms can partly shape popularity rather than merely measure it.
